title: Tell first-run operators that a codex seat is interactive and lands nothing until it is closed
description:
DOCS ONLY. Measured on 2026-09-11 against the current working tree.

The first-run path offers codex as a one-line swap and says nothing about how a codex seat actually behaves. README.md line ~148 (inside the collapsed "Launch agents from external terminals" block) says only: "These examples use Claude Code. For Codex, add `-Command codex` on Windows or `--command codex` on macOS/Linux." docs/GETTING_STARTED.md repeats it twice, at line 31 for the installer and line 85 for the launch commands. Neither mentions two facts an operator hits within minutes.

FACT 1 - a codex seat is INTERACTIVE for every role by default. scripts/moe-agent.sh line 394 states it outright ("Codex is interactive (TUI) for every role unless --codex-exec opts the seat"), and the PowerShell twin resolves -CodexExec the same way. So a first-run operator who follows the quick start gets a terminal UI, not the headless one-shot loop the rest of the quick start implicitly describes.

FACT 2 - a terminal-UI seat lands its commits only when the operator CLOSES the UI. The wrapper's post-flight is what makes the completion or checkpoint commit, and it runs after the CLI exits. So a codex seat left open finishes its task on the board while nothing is committed, which reads exactly like the auto-commit being broken. This is the practical trap, and the quick start is where it needs saying, because the quick start explicitly tells the reader to "review the changed files and recorded commit in Git".

FACT 3 - an asymmetry in the flag reference. docs/DEVELOPMENT.md line 174 documents `-GrokExec` / `--grok-exec`, including that it exists for roles that default to the interactive TUI. There is NO corresponding `-CodexExec` / `--codex-exec` entry, even though the flag exists in both wrappers (bash help text at scripts/moe-agent.sh line 299) and codex has the same TUI default.

WHAT IS ALREADY FINE - do not duplicate it. docs/CONFIGURATION.md line 55 covers MOE_CODEX_SANDBOX, its danger-full-access default, the measured reasons for that default, the pinned tools-approval mode on the moe and serena servers, and that --full-auto is never passed. docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md lines 291-343 cover the same ground plus the Windows sandbox failure. Those are the right homes for the detail. This card adds a short first-run warning and one missing flag entry, and links to those pages rather than restating them.

Scope: README.md, docs/GETTING_STARTED.md, docs/DEVELOPMENT.md (3 files). No script, no behaviour, no test change - nothing here alters what any wrapper executes.

NOT IN SCOPE: changing the codex TUI default (that was reverted to interactive deliberately on 2026-09-07 and is not being relitigated here), adding a --yolo flag to codex (codex has none; --full-auto was removed in codex-cli 0.147 and parity-check fails on its reintroduction), and restating the sandbox or approval detail that CONFIGURATION.md already owns.

Verification: npm run lint from the repository root (bash script, so Git Bash on Windows) must exit 0, and a grep must show each of the three files naming the codex exec flag. There is no docs test harness, so state plainly in the completion summary that the remaining check is a human read.
definitionOfDone: README.md's launch section states that a codex seat runs the interactive terminal UI by default and that such a seat commits nothing until the operator closes it, and names the -CodexExec / --codex-exec flag as the unattended alternative.
docs/GETTING_STARTED.md carries the same warning wherever it currently offers codex as a swap (around lines 31 and 85), phrased once and cross-referenced rather than duplicated in both places.
docs/DEVELOPMENT.md documents -CodexExec / --codex-exec in the same flag-reference style as the existing -GrokExec / --grok-exec entry at line 174, closing that asymmetry.

The sandbox, approval-policy and --full-auto detail already in docs/CONFIGURATION.md line 55 and docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md is LINKED, not restated; no contradiction is introduced between the four documents.
No script, no test and no behaviour changed: git diff touches only the three documentation files.
npm run lint exits 0, and the command plus a grep showing the flag named in all three files is recorded in the completion verification.
taskRails: Documentation only: do not change the codex TUI default, any wrapper argv, or any test.
Do not restate what docs/CONFIGURATION.md and docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md already own; link to them.
Do not claim codex has a yolo flag. It does not, and --full-auto is rejected by codex-cli 0.147+ and guarded by parity-check.

implementationPlan.description: ADD THE FIRST-RUN WARNING TO README.md. Extend the existing sentence at line 145 so an operator choosing codex learns three things in the place they actually decide: a codex seat runs the interactive terminal UI for every role by default; such a seat does not commit anything until the operator closes it, because the launcher makes its commit after the CLI exits; and -CodexExec on Windows or --codex-exec elsewhere is the unattended alternative that lands a commit per task. The second point is the one that earns its place here and it should be the emphasis, because the quick start tells the reader a few lines earlier to 'review the changed files and recorded commit in Git' - which is exactly the check that looks broken when a terminal-UI seat is still open. Frame it as what the operator will SEE, not as an internal mechanism: the task reaches Done on the board while Git shows nothing yet. Keep it to two or three sentences inside the existing collapsed block; this is a first-run page and a wall of caveats there is its own failure. Link the sandbox and approval detail to docs/CONFIGURATION.md rather than restating any of it. Do not describe codex as having a yolo mode, and do not name the bypass-approvals flag - whether Moe should ever offer that is a separate decision and this card must not pre-empt it.

comments.content:
VERIFIED AGAINST THE INSTALLED CLI, 2026-09-11. codex-cli 0.154.0. This supersedes the third task rail, which is too absolute.

`codex exec --help` reports:

    -s, --sandbox <SANDBOX_MODE>
        [possible values: read-only, workspace-write, danger-full-access]

So `danger-full-access` is real and is one of exactly three accepted values. The wrapper's default is a genuine flag value, not an invention, and `MOE_CODEX_SANDBOX` is a real dial the operator can turn down to `workspace-write` or `read-only`.

`--full-auto` returns zero matches in the exec help, confirming the repository's claim that codex-cli 0.147 removed it and that the wrapper is right never to pass it.

THE CORRECTION. codex 0.154.0 DOES carry a bypass-everything flag, present both at top level and under exec:

    --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox
        Skip all confirmation prompts and execute commands without sandboxing. EXTREMELY
        DANGEROUS. Intended solely for running in environments that are externally sandboxed

That is codex's actual yolo-equivalent. So the accurate statement is: codex has no flag NAMED yolo, but it does have this one, and the wrapper deliberately does not use it. The wrapper instead relies on `exec` implying an approval policy of never, plus `--sandbox danger-full-access`. The practical difference is worth a sentence somewhere: the bypass flag removes both the approval plumbing and the sandbox dial, whereas the wrapper's spelling keeps `MOE_CODEX_SANDBOX` meaningful so an operator can still restrict a seat.

Treat the third rail as amended to: do not claim codex has a `--yolo` flag, and do not introduce `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox` as part of a documentation card. Whether the wrapper should ever offer it is a separate decision with a separate card, and this docs task must not make it.

Also worth documenting if it is cheap: `--approve-for-me` is new in this version and routes approvals through automatic review under the workspace-write sandbox. Not required by this card's Definition of Done; mention it only if it fits the flag reference naturally.

Board note, not a defect to repair by hand: this row came back `createdBy: WORKER` even though an architect workerId was supplied. Same quirk recorded on the 2026-09-10 decomposition cards.
